assertions: DEX is unpaused (dexVariables2 high bit == 0)
Both smart-collateral and smart-debt pools are enabled
dexVariables (last-stored swap price/oracle slot) is at attacker-favorable boundary
setup_calls: attacker funds MaliciousCallbackContract with sufficient tokenIn
attacker pre-positions a perfect-deposit position so that subsequent _withdrawPerfect / borrowPerfect path is reachable from the callback

attack_steps: Attacker calls FluidDexT1.swapInWithCallback(...) from MaliciousCallbackContract.

Inside _swapIn, after price/reserves are computed from current dexVariables but BEFORE dexVariables are written back via _updateOracle (line ~354), the dex calls LIQUIDITY.operate which triggers a liquidityCallback on the dex; the dex then invokes IDexCallback(msg.sender).dexCallback(token_, amount_) on the attacker contract to pull tokenIn.

At callback time, the dex has not yet updated dexVariables for this trade. Attacker re-enters via a different external entry — either (a) FluidDexT1.depositPerfect / borrowPerfect (which routes through PERFECT_OPERATIONS_AND_SWAP_OUT_IMPLEMENTATION via _spell delegatecall and may share the same dexVariables read), or (b) another swap path that uses the stale pex_ snapshot.

If the inner state read happens against pre-trade reserves but trades settle against post-trade liquidity balances, attacker pays old-price for a portion already locked in flight — extracting price/exchange-price difference.

The same callback entry-point is also reachable mid-flight in swapOutWithCallback via the same _spell route; combined with the dexCallback pulling tokens, attacker can momentarily owe tokens it has not transferred, expanding the inconsistent-state window.
preconditions: Attacker has tokenIn equal to required amountIn
Pool reserves are large enough that an in-flight swap is meaningful relative to dexVariables drift

triage.drop_reason: Verification not performed in this iteration (15-iter budget; mainnet-fork PoC against full Fluid stack would consume ~all of it). Rationale: dex calls IDexCallback(msg.sender).dexCallback during _swapIn before _updateOracle writes the post-trade dexVariables. Two LIQUIDITY.operate calls are made in sequence; the first one's liquidityCallback yields control to the dex and then to msg.sender. The 'reentrancy bit' pattern visible in vaultT1.liquidate (vaultVariables & 1) is the canonical lock used in this codebase, but FluidDexT1._swapIn does not exhibit a similar guard at the entry point — instead relying on dexVariables only being committed at the end, which is the pattern that has historically caused mid-flight oracle/state bugs (e.g., curve-style read-only reentrancy). Needs deeper trace through PERFECT_OPERATIONS_AND_SWAP_OUT_IMPLEMENTATION._spell and a PoC that exploits stale pex_ snapshot. KG seed: BNO_exp (2023-07) — interface-overlap match (IERC20/IERC721) plus general callback-during-state pattern. MCGA: dexCallback ranks #6 by sink density with combined block_dep + transfer_token + unchecked_arith sinks.

deployments: deploy:MaliciousCenterPriceContract implementing ICenterPrice.centerPrice() returning attacker-controlled value

assertions: DEX has a non-zero centerPriceContract configured in dexVariables2 (i.e., extracted external center-price source is enabled)
Range shifting is currently active (rangeShift_ has nonzero startTimeStamp_/shiftDuration_)
block.timestamp is near the boundary (startTimeStamp_ + shiftDuration_) of the active shift
setup_calls: attacker observes that dexVariables2 references an external ICenterPrice contract whose price is permitted to drift
attacker times tx so that (startTimeStamp_ + shiftDuration_) < block.timestamp by a small delta

attack_steps: Step 1: monitor rangeShift slot. When (startTimeStamp_ + shiftDuration_) just crosses block.timestamp, _calcRangeShifting takes the 'shifting fully done' branch and applies the target upperRange/lowerRange in full — but only on the next state-mutating call.

Step 2: in the same block (or via a flashloan), call swapIn at the boundary so that pex_ (PricesAndExchangePrices) is computed using the just-finalized range. Because _calcShiftingDone uses linear `((diff_ * timePassed_) / shiftDuration_)` integer division, on the boundary block the value snaps abruptly from interpolated to final without a smoothing window.

Step 3: combine with a center-price contract whose value moves freely — _updateOracle commits a new price based on this jump. The next observer of dexVariables (e.g. liquidations or downstream resolvers reading via DexT1) sees a price that moved more in 1 block than the shift duration was supposed to allow.

Step 4: on the post-jump block, attacker's pre-positioned LP shares or perfect-deposit position is redeemable at the inflated post-jump price; the symmetric victim is anyone whose collateral is valued via the dex price (FluidVaults using DexOracle implementations).
preconditions: ICenterPrice contract is referenced via dexVariables2 (configurable per-pool by admin)
An active range/threshold shift exists at attack time
Attacker has access to flashloan liquidity to amplify the boundary-block opportunity

triage.drop_reason: Verification not performed in this iteration. Rationale: _calcShiftingDone uses linear integer interpolation `current_ = old_ + ((diff_ * timePassed_) / shiftDuration_)` which is monotonic but discontinuous at the boundary because the 'shifting done' branch (line 73-80) snaps the dexVariables2 storage in one shot. Combined with an external ICenterPrice contract that the dex trusts without staleness checks (the interface only exposes `centerPrice()` view, no timestamp or signed bound), a malicious or compromised admin-configured center-price contract can return values that, in the boundary block, get committed to dexVariables via _updateOracle without being smoothed against a previous-block bound. MCGA: _calcRangeShifting tops the external sink-density list with 23 sinks (block_dep + unchecked_arith) — the block_dep tags are exactly these timestamp-boundary reads. KG seed: not a direct DeFiHackLabs match, but pattern resembles oracle-trust assumption attacks generally found in the IChainlinkAggregatorV3 interface family (target imports it). Severity is medium-to-high IF an external centerPrice contract is in use; otherwise informational.

assertions: Borrower position is at currentTick > maxTick (above max-limit liquidation tick) so absorb branch is taken
Oracle.getExchangeRateLiquidate() returns a value such that capped-to-1e45 path is exercised (temp_ > 1e45 capping branch)
Liquidation penalty (vaultVariables2 >> 72) & X10 is at maximum (1023 → 10.23%)
BORROW_TOKEN is a low-decimal token (e.g., USDC 6dp) so that the supplyExPrice / borrowExPrice ratio multiplier interacts with the cap
setup_calls: ensure borrower is at the absorb threshold by warping price slightly past maxTick
attacker pre-funds debt token to liquidate

attack_steps: Observe borrower whose position has tick > maxTick. liquidate() will absorb up to maxTick first via _spell to SECONDARY_IMPLEMENTATION.absorb.

Inside the unchecked block at L644-L676, temp_ is converted from oracle exchange rate × supplyExPrice / borrowExPrice; cap `if (temp_ > 1e45) temp_ = 1e45` is applied AFTER the multiplication, so any overflow during the multiplication itself silently wraps before the cap is read.

When supplyExPrice / borrowExPrice is large (e.g., long-lived borrow with steep interest accrual), `temp_ * supplyExPrice` can wrap inside unchecked even if the original oracle price was well below the cap; the post-wrap value then trivially passes the `if (temp_ > 1e45)` check (because the wrapped value is small) and is used directly in `temp2_ = 1e54 / temp_`, yielding an inflated colPerDebt_ that pays the liquidator more collateral than the protocol intends.
Attacker calls liquidate() with this skewed colPerDebt; profit = (inflated colPerDebt - true colPerDebt) × debtAmt × (1 + penalty).
preconditions: Vault has been live long enough for supplyExPrice / borrowExPrice to grow significantly (1e36+ scale)

triage.drop_reason: Verification not performed in this iteration. Rationale: the `unchecked` block at L644-L676 of vaultT1/main.sol contains chained multiplications `temp_ = (temp_ * supplyExPrice) / borrowExPrice` followed by `temp2_ = 1e54 / temp_` followed by `temp2_ * (10000 + penalty)`. The 1e45 cap fires AFTER the first multiplication, not before. With temp_ near 1e54 (oracle returns up to 1e54 per the validity check at L640) and supplyExPrice up to ~1e30 in long-lived markets, `temp_ * supplyExPrice` exceeds 2^256 and wraps inside unchecked. Whether this actually under-pays the protocol vs over-pays depends on which direction the wrap pushes temp_ relative to colPerDebt scaling — needs a forge fuzz to nail down. MCGA: limiting.liquidate ranks #2 with 22 unchecked_arith sinks; FluidVault._liquidate internal callee ranks #1 with 20. KG seed: no direct DeFiHackLabs match — generic unchecked-overflow pattern. Severity highly conditional on real-world supplyExPrice values reaching the wrap boundary; if Fluid auditors verified bounds, this is informational.
